title: Firewall consoles compromised, BlueMoon spreads, and an example key
overview: Cisco confirms attacks on its firewall management console, while Fortinet and Citrix face Saturday federal patch deadlines. BlueMoon connects yesterday's Windows flaw to browser-based espionage, and exposed LiteLLM gateways reveal the cost of copying an example admin key.
paragraphs: [cheerful] Good morning, it's 5:00 AM. Thursday, the tenth of September, twenty twenty-six. five twenty-two AM is brought to you by Lab five twenty-two, a technology partner for mid-market businesses, providing cyber security services and enterprise operational software. Email us at hello at lab five twenty-two dot co dot uk if you think we can help your business.

[serious] The console that manages your Cisco firewalls can now be somebody else's console. Cisco confirmed yesterday that CVE-2026-20079, patched in March, is being exploited. It scores ten: an improper process created at boot lets crafted web requests run scripts as root in Secure Firewall Management Center, without a login. That's the machine trusted to push firewall policy. [short pause] Talos found credential theft, and a Sandworm-linked cluster chaining the bypass with static credentials to deploy Cyclops Blink. A Qilin ransomware operator used those credentials to build an encryption target list.

[curious] What bugs me is the timing: Cisco says it knew in August, while its example log indicator is dated the twenty-third of July. [confident] If you run F-M-C, take its web interface off the internet and apply both Cisco hotfixes; there aren't any workarounds. The cloud-hosted Security Cloud Control service is already patched. Search slash var slash log slash messages for activity involving slash var slash tmp slash license dot tmp. Finding it means treating the box as compromised, not merely overdue an update. Federal agencies have until Saturday, the twelfth. A hardening release is due next week; I wouldn't wait for it.

[serious] Same old-patch problem at Fortinet: attackers are exploiting January's CVE-2025-25249 to plant PivotC2 on FortiGate appliances. Crafted requests trigger a heap overflow without authentication; the backdoor gives them a shell and tunnels into the network. SOCRadar counted a hundred and seventy-eight infected devices, with data stolen in at least two intrusions. [calm] Federal agencies have the same Saturday deadline. For FortiOS, the fixed destinations are 7 point 0 point 18 or 7 point 2 point 12 on those branches; on newer branches, 7 point 4 point 9 or 7 point 6 point 4. FortiSwitchManager needs 7 point 0 point 6 or 7 point 2 point 7, or newer. If a box has sat unpatched since January, investigate it before trusting it again.

[long pause] [curious] Yesterday's Windows A-L-P-C flaw now has a delivery chain attached. Proofpoint calls it BlueMoon: four espionage clusters, most with suspected China links, using practically identical code since the twenty-eighth of August. Phishing links lead to a page chaining two Chrome V8 bugs for execution and sandbox escape, then the Windows flaw raises privileges. [serious] Both browser bugs were fixed in public Chromium code before stable Chrome caught up. That's an uncomfortable window for defenders. Get Chrome to 153 point 0 point 8010 point 36 or later, alongside the Windows fix we discussed yesterday. Then hunt for chrome dot exe launching cmd dot exe, followed by curl dot exe and msgbox dot exe. Proofpoint has host indicators and network signatures; updating the browser doesn't remove a payload already installed.

[serious] Back at the network edge, ransomware crews are now exploiting WatchGuard Firebox CVE-2025-14733, with nearly nine thousand boxes still unsecured nine months after the patch. Install December's Fireware fixes and check WatchGuard's compromise indicators, including branch-office V-P-N configuration with a static gateway peer even if I-K-E version two has been removed. [short pause] And Citrix NetScaler A-D-C and Gateway have an exploited authentication bypass, CVE-2026-19490, with that same Saturday federal deadline. Affected branches run through 14 point 1 build 73 point 32 and 13 point 1 build 63 point 21; move to a fixed release beyond those ranges, then review sessions and administrator accounts.

[curious] On Windows, being fully patched isn't enough for ShieldCrash: Nightmare Eclipse's published proof of concept demonstrates arbitrary file reads as System despite September's updates, bypassing Microsoft's third-of-September ShieldBreak fix. [serious] The researcher claims full System access and S-A-M database dumping too; there's no patch, so enable tamper protection. [short pause] And in A-I infrastructure, Wiz found two hundred and ninety-four exposed LiteLLM gateways accepting the guide's example admin key, sk dash one two three four; a hundred and ninety-one had no key set and would've accepted anything, while the guide still used that example yesterday. If you run LiteLLM, the gateway between applications and model providers, check the separate salt-key setting before rotating the master key so stored credentials remain readable, and upgrade to 1 point 84 point 0 or later for the separate exploited flaws, including an M-C-P bypass with a federal deadline of the sixteenth; restrict outbound access and cloud permissions too, because the pass-through route to instance metadata has no patch.

[confident] I'd put an exposed firewall-management console ahead of routine rollout work today. And I'd keep the incident investigation open after the update succeeds — a successful installer isn't a clean bill of health. [cheerful] Enjoy the rest of your morning. five twenty-two AM, brought to you by Lab five twenty-two. Find us at lab five twenty-two dot co dot uk.
